title: React Mastery: From Fundamentals to Production Architecture
subtitle: A deep, example-driven React course covering rendering, state, effects, hooks, forms, context, performance, routing, testing, accessibility, and senior-level architecture.

chapters.title: React Mental Model and Rendering
chapters.summary: Build the correct mental model for React before learning APIs: declarative UI, component trees, renders, reconciliation, identity, and the browser commit phase.

sections.title: Why React Exists
sections.content:
React is primarily a way to describe how UI should look for a given application state. Instead of manually finding DOM nodes and issuing a sequence of mutations, you describe the desired UI as a function of data.

The important shift is from **imperative UI programming** to **declarative UI programming**.

In an imperative approach you might say: find the counter element, read its text, add one, and write the result back. In React, you store the count as state and describe that the heading should contain the current count. When state changes, React determines what needs to change in the DOM.

React does not mean that the browser is rebuilt on every update. React creates and compares representations of the UI, then commits the necessary DOM changes. Understanding this distinction becomes important when reasoning about performance.

codeExample.title: Why React Exists — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: React lets you describe UI from state rather than manually synchronizing DOM nodes.
A render calculates what the UI should be; the commit phase applies necessary host changes.
Declarative code reduces the amount of synchronization logic you have to maintain.

sections.title: Components, Trees, and Rendering
sections.content:
A React application can be understood as a tree of components. A parent component returns elements that may contain child components, and those children can return further elements.

A **render** means React calls the relevant component functions to calculate the next UI description. A render does not automatically mean the browser DOM changed. React can render, compare the result, and discover that no host mutation is required.

A useful debugging question is therefore: “What caused this component to render?” rather than “What changed in the DOM?” The answer might be state, changed props, a parent render, context, or another mechanism.

Component functions should be treated as calculations. During render, avoid side effects such as network requests, subscriptions, timers, or direct DOM mutations.

codeExample.title: Components, Trees, and Rendering — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Component functions describe UI and should remain free of side effects during render.
A render is not synonymous with a DOM update.
Think of React as maintaining a tree of UI descriptions whose output is committed to the host environment.

sections.title: Reconciliation, Identity, and Keys
sections.content:
When React receives a new element tree, it needs to determine which existing elements can be reused and which need to be replaced. Element type and identity are central to this process.

Keys are especially important for arrays. A key tells React which item is which across renders. A stable key such as a database ID allows React to preserve the identity of an item even when its position changes.

Using an array index as a key is not always wrong, but it becomes dangerous when the list can be reordered, filtered, inserted into, or deleted from. In those situations the index describes a position, not the identity of the underlying item.

diagram.title: Render to Commit
diagram.code:
flowchart LR
A[State or Props Change] --> B[Render Components]
B --> C[Element Tree]
C --> D[Reconciliation]
D --> E[Commit Necessary Host Changes]
E --> F[Browser UI]

codeExample.title: Reconciliation, Identity, and Keys — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Keys represent item identity within a sibling list.
Stable keys help React preserve component state when list positions change.
Do not choose a key merely because it is convenient; choose one that identifies the data item.

sections.title: Strict Mode and Render Purity
sections.content:
`StrictMode` enables development-time checks that help expose unsafe assumptions. One of the most useful effects is making certain render/effect behavior more visible during development.

This can make code appear to run more than once, but it is not a reason to add arbitrary guards such as `hasRunRef.current`. Instead, make rendering pure and make effects safe to start, clean up, and restart.

A pure component produces the same JSX for the same inputs and does not mutate external state while rendering. Event handlers and effects are appropriate places for interactions and synchronization.

callout.title: Debugging habit
callout.message: If an effect behaves incorrectly when setup is followed immediately by cleanup and setup again, the effect usually has a lifecycle bug rather than React having a bug.

codeExample.title: Strict Mode and Render Purity — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Development behavior under Strict Mode is intended to reveal unsafe patterns.
Do not solve Strict Mode behavior with arbitrary one-time flags.
Render should be pure; effects should be resilient to setup and cleanup.

sections.title: Reconciliation Heuristics
sections.content:
React does not solve arbitrary tree-diffing optimally. It uses practical heuristics based on element types, positions, and keys. If two sibling elements have the same type, React can often reuse their existing representation; if their types differ, the corresponding subtree may be replaced.

The key lesson is not to memorize an implementation algorithm. Instead, understand that identity is what lets React preserve state and avoid unnecessary replacement.
keyTakeaways: Element type and key identity influence whether existing component state can be preserved.
Do not depend on undocumented reconciliation details beyond stable public semantics.

sections.title: State Preservation and Identity
sections.content:
State belongs to a component's position and identity in the rendered tree. Changing a key can deliberately give a subtree a new identity and therefore reset its state.

This is useful for editors, forms, and resource-specific screens where switching from one logical entity to another should start with fresh local state.

codeExample.title: State Preservation and Identity — Example
codeExample.explanation: A practical example of the concept.

keyTakeaways: Keys are an identity mechanism, not merely list metadata.
Changing identity can intentionally reset local state.

sections.title: Render Purity and Idempotence
sections.content:
Render functions can be called more than once and a render can be abandoned before commit. Therefore rendering must not perform irreversible operations such as sending analytics, mutating external stores, or starting timers.

If something must happen because the user clicked, put it in the event handler. If something must synchronize with an external system after commit, use an Effect.
keyTakeaways: Never make render responsible for irreversible side effects.
Purity is essential to modern React scheduling.

chapters.title: JSX, Components, Props, and Composition
chapters.summary: Learn how JSX maps to JavaScript, how components receive data, and how composition produces reusable UI without creating rigid component APIs.

sections.title: JSX Is a JavaScript Syntax Extension
sections.content:
JSX is not HTML embedded in a separate language runtime. It is syntax that is transformed into JavaScript calls that describe elements.

JSX attributes use JavaScript expressions inside `{}`. Most values that are not strings are passed as expressions. `className` is used instead of HTML's `class`, and event props use camelCase names such as `onClick`.

Understanding JSX as JavaScript makes advanced patterns less mysterious: conditional expressions, mapping arrays, spreading props, fragments, and component composition all follow normal JavaScript rules.

codeExample.title: JSX Is a JavaScript Syntax Extension — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: JSX expressions inside braces are evaluated as JavaScript.
JSX produces React elements; it is not a template language that directly mutates the DOM.
Normal JavaScript concepts such as arrays, expressions, and functions remain central to JSX.

sections.title: Props and One-Way Data Flow
sections.content:
Props are inputs supplied by a parent to a child. A child should generally treat props as read-only values and communicate user actions upward through callbacks.

This creates a predictable data flow: parent state flows down, events flow up. If multiple components need to coordinate around the same piece of state, move that state to their closest common owner rather than duplicating it.

A common beginner mistake is copying props into state without a synchronization strategy. That creates two sources of truth and can easily produce stale UI.

codeExample.title: Props and One-Way Data Flow — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Props flow from parent to child.
Callbacks are a common way for children to request changes owned by a parent.
Avoid duplicating a prop in state unless there is a deliberate reason and synchronization model.

sections.title: Composition and the `children` Prop
sections.content:
Reusable components become easier to maintain when they expose extension points rather than dozens of boolean or configuration props.

React's `children` prop lets a component wrap arbitrary content. More advanced composition can use named props containing elements, render functions, or compound component patterns.

The goal is to keep ownership clear. A `Card` should own card layout, while the caller can decide what content belongs inside it. This avoids creating a separate prop for every possible variation.

codeExample.title: Composition and the `children` Prop — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Composition lets reusable components control structure without owning every piece of content.
`children` is simply a prop containing nested React content.
Prefer composable APIs when a component is accumulating many mutually interacting configuration props.

sections.title: Conditional and List Rendering
sections.content:
React uses normal JavaScript expressions for conditional rendering. Use ternaries when there are two explicit alternatives and logical `&&` when a value should be shown only when a condition is truthy.

When rendering collections, `map()` transforms data into elements. Always consider what happens when the collection is empty and whether the key is stable.

Be careful with `condition && value`: if `condition` can be `0`, the number `0` may be rendered. For numeric conditions, an explicit comparison is often clearer.

codeExample.title: Conditional and List Rendering — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Conditional rendering is ordinary JavaScript combined with JSX.
Use stable keys when rendering collections.
Explicit conditions are safer when falsy values such as `0` or an empty string have meaning.

sections.title: Prop Drilling and When It Is Actually a Problem
sections.content:
Passing props through one or two layers is usually simple and explicit. Prop drilling becomes a problem when many unrelated intermediate components must forward a value they do not use.

Before introducing Context, ask whether the intermediate components are actually expressing a useful ownership relationship. Context is best when the dependency is genuinely cross-cutting.
keyTakeaways: Prop passing is not inherently bad.
Use Context when many descendants need the same coherent dependency.

sections.title: Component API Stability
sections.content:
A component API is a contract. Changing a prop from a boolean to a union, changing whether a callback is optional, or changing controlled/uncontrolled behavior can affect many consumers.

Reusable components should document defaults, accessibility guarantees, controlled behavior, and supported composition patterns.
keyTakeaways: Treat reusable component props as public APIs.
Prefer constrained variants over arbitrary strings.

sections.title: Render Props Versus Hooks
sections.content:
Render props were historically a powerful way to share stateful behavior. Hooks now cover many of those use cases with less nesting.

Render props remain useful when the reusable abstraction owns an interaction lifecycle while consumers need complete control over the rendered output. Choose the simpler abstraction for the actual requirement.

codeExample.title: Render Props Versus Hooks — Example
codeExample.explanation: A practical example of the concept.

keyTakeaways: Hooks are often the simpler modern abstraction.
Render props remain valid when rendering control is the primary requirement.

chapters.title: State, Events, and Interactive UI
chapters.summary: Understand state as React-managed memory, event handling, functional updates, batching, immutable updates, and controlled inputs.

sections.title: State Is Component Memory
sections.content:
`useState` gives a component a value that persists between renders and a setter that requests a new render.

Calling a state setter does not immediately change the current render's variable. The current render is a snapshot. The next render receives the new state.

This explains why code such as `setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1);` usually results in one increment: both calculations read the same `count` from the current render. When the next value depends on the previous value, use the functional updater form.

codeExample.title: State Is Component Memory — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Each render sees a snapshot of state.
Use functional updates when calculating new state from previous state.
A setter schedules an update; it does not mutate the current render's variable.

sections.title: Updating Objects and Arrays Immutably
sections.content:
React state should be treated as immutable. The practical reason is not that JavaScript objects are magically immutable; it is that replacing values with new references gives React and your code a reliable way to reason about changes.

For objects, create a new object with spread syntax. For arrays, use methods such as `map`, `filter`, and spread rather than mutating methods like `push` or `splice` on the existing state array.

Immer can make immutable updates easier for complex state, but the underlying model remains the same: produce the next state without mutating the existing snapshot.

codeExample.title: Updating Objects and Arrays Immutably — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Do not mutate existing state objects or arrays in place.
Create new references for changed structures.
Functional updates are useful when the next state depends on the previous snapshot.

sections.title: Event Handling and Event Boundaries
sections.content:
React event props receive functions. Pass the function reference rather than calling it during render.

Event handlers are an appropriate place for imperative actions that directly respond to user interaction: opening a dialog, starting a request, changing state, or calling a browser API.

Keep the event handler focused on the interaction. If the same business operation can happen from multiple entry points, extract the underlying operation so the event handler is not the only place where important domain logic exists.

codeExample.title: Event Handling and Event Boundaries — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Pass event handlers as functions such as `onClick={handleClick}`.
Do not use `onClick={handleClick()}` unless the function call itself is intentionally part of rendering.
Separate UI event handling from reusable domain operations when complexity grows.

sections.title: Controlled Inputs and Form State
sections.content:
A controlled input gets its current value from React state and reports changes through an event handler. This makes React the source of truth for the input.

Controlled forms are useful when validation, conditional fields, formatting, or submission state needs to be coordinated. For very large forms, libraries can reduce repetitive state management, but understanding controlled inputs is still essential.

For numeric inputs, remember that `event.target.value` is still a string. Parse it deliberately rather than assuming it is already a number.

codeExample.title: Controlled Inputs and Form State — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: A controlled input gets its value from React state.
Prevent default form submission when handling submission in React.
Input values are strings unless you explicitly parse them.

chapters.title: Effects, Refs, and External Systems
chapters.summary: Learn when effects are actually needed, how dependency arrays work, how cleanup prevents leaks, and how refs bridge React with imperative systems.

sections.title: Effects Synchronize With External Systems
sections.content:
An Effect is for synchronizing React with something outside React: a WebSocket, browser subscription, timer, imperative widget, network synchronization process, or another external system.

Effects are often overused for derived data. If a value can be calculated from props or state during render, calculate it during render instead of storing it in state and updating it from an Effect.

A strong rule is: **if there is no external system to synchronize with, you probably do not need an Effect.**

callout.title: Common anti-pattern
callout.message: Avoid `const [fullName, setFullName] = useState(...)` followed by an Effect that recalculates fullName from firstName and lastName. That value can be derived during render.

codeExample.title: Effects Synchronize With External Systems — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Effects are synchronization mechanisms, not general-purpose lifecycle callbacks.
Derived values should normally be calculated during render.
An Effect should have a clear external system or imperative boundary it synchronizes with.

sections.title: Dependency Arrays and Closures
sections.content:
An Effect closes over values from the render in which it was created. The dependency array tells React which reactive values the Effect uses and therefore when it must be synchronized again.

A missing dependency can create stale closures. For example, an interval callback can keep reading an old state value if that state is omitted from the dependencies.

Do not treat the dependency array as a performance knob where dependencies are removed until an Effect runs less often. Instead, restructure the code so the Effect has correct dependencies and a clear synchronization boundary.

codeExample.title: Dependency Arrays and Closures — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Effect callbacks capture values from their render.
Dependencies should represent the reactive values used by the Effect.
Functional state updates can avoid unnecessary dependencies when only the previous state is needed.

sections.title: Cleanup, Cancellation, and Race Conditions
sections.content:
Effects that create resources must clean them up. Timers need clearing, subscriptions need unsubscribing, and browser listeners need removal.

Data fetching introduces another issue: an older request may finish after a newer request. If its result is applied unconditionally, stale data can overwrite current data. An `AbortController` can cancel fetches when an Effect is cleaned up.

Cleanup is not only about preventing memory leaks. It also prevents obsolete work from affecting current UI state.

codeExample.title: Cleanup, Cancellation, and Race Conditions — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Cleanup should reverse the resource acquisition performed by the Effect.
Abort or otherwise invalidate obsolete asynchronous work.
Race conditions are correctness bugs, not merely performance issues.

sections.title: Refs: Persistent Mutable Values and DOM Access
sections.content:
`useRef` returns a stable object whose `.current` property can change without causing a render.

A ref is appropriate for values that must survive renders but do not themselves determine what should be displayed: DOM nodes, timer IDs, previous values, or imperative library instances.

A ref is not a replacement for state. If changing the value should update the UI, use state. If the value is an implementation detail that should not trigger rendering, a ref can be appropriate.

codeExample.title: Refs: Persistent Mutable Values and DOM Access — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Refs persist values between renders without scheduling renders when `.current` changes.
Use refs for imperative DOM access and non-visual mutable values.
Use state for values that participate in rendered output.

sections.title: Effect Lifecycle With Changing Dependencies
sections.content:
When an Effect dependency changes, React conceptually transitions from the old synchronization to the new one: cleanup for the previous setup, followed by setup for the new values.

This is why cleanup should close over the same resource identity that setup created. A cleanup that references a newer mutable value can accidentally disconnect the wrong resource.
keyTakeaways: Cleanup belongs to the setup that created the resource.
Avoid mutable global variables for subscription identity.

sections.title: Layout Effects Versus Effects
sections.content:
`useLayoutEffect` runs after DOM mutations but before the browser paints, which makes it useful for measuring layout or synchronously adjusting DOM before the user sees it.

It can block painting, so ordinary synchronization should prefer `useEffect`. Use layout effects only when visual correctness requires pre-paint work.

codeExample.title: Layout Effects Versus Effects — Example
codeExample.explanation: A practical example of the concept.

keyTakeaways: Prefer `useEffect` unless pre-paint DOM measurement is required.
Layout effects can block visual updates.

sections.title: Callback Refs
sections.content:
Callback refs are useful when code needs to react immediately to a DOM node being attached or detached. Unlike an object ref, the callback receives the node itself and can perform setup around the attachment lifecycle.

They are particularly useful for integrating third-party imperative APIs that need an element as soon as it exists.

codeExample.title: Callback Refs — Example
codeExample.explanation: A practical example of the concept.

keyTakeaways: Callback refs are useful for imperative node attachment.
Keep cleanup tied to the resource created for that node.

chapters.title: Hooks Deep Dive and Custom Hooks
chapters.summary: Master the rules of hooks, memoization hooks, reducers, stable callbacks, custom hooks, and how to design hook APIs around behavior.

sections.title: Rules of Hooks
sections.content:
Hooks must be called at the top level of a React function component or another custom Hook. Do not call them conditionally, inside loops, or inside nested callbacks.

React relies on the consistent ordering of Hook calls to associate each call with its stored state. Changing the order between renders breaks that association.

A custom Hook is simply a function whose name begins with `use` and that can call other Hooks. It is a way to reuse stateful behavior, not a special component type.

codeExample.title: Rules of Hooks — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Hooks must be called consistently at the top level.
Custom Hooks reuse behavior and stateful logic.
Hook rules are structural requirements, not stylistic preferences.

sections.title: When `useReducer` Fits Better Than Multiple State Setters
sections.content:
`useReducer` centralizes transitions for related state. It is useful when state changes have meaningful events or when several values must change together.

A reducer should be a pure function: `(state, action) => nextState`. It should not perform network requests, access the DOM, or mutate external systems.

Reducers make state transitions explicit and testable. They can also make complex components easier to reason about because event handlers dispatch domain-level actions instead of manually updating several fields.

codeExample.title: When `useReducer` Fits Better Than Multiple State Setters — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Reducers make related state transitions explicit.
Keep reducers pure and deterministic.
Actions should describe events or domain transitions rather than UI implementation details.

sections.title: Memoization with `useMemo` and `useCallback`
sections.content:
`useMemo` caches a calculated value and `useCallback` caches a function identity. Neither should be used simply because a component has many renders.

Memoization helps when a calculation is genuinely expensive or when stable identity matters to a memoized child or another dependency boundary.

Adding memoization everywhere increases cognitive complexity. Measure first, then optimize the specific render or computation that matters.

codeExample.title: Memoization with `useMemo` and `useCallback` — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: `useMemo` caches a value; `useCallback` caches a function identity.
Memoization is useful when it removes measurable work or prevents meaningful downstream rerenders.
Do not use memoization as a substitute for understanding why a component renders.

sections.title: Designing Useful Custom Hooks
sections.content:
A good custom Hook exposes a behavior-oriented API. It should hide implementation details while returning the smallest useful interface.

For example, `useDebouncedValue(value, delay)` communicates intent better than exposing timer IDs and internal state. A Hook can combine state, effects, refs, and callbacks behind a simple contract.

Custom Hooks should not secretly introduce surprising global behavior. Document ownership, cleanup, and whether the Hook creates a shared or per-component resource.

codeExample.title: Designing Useful Custom Hooks — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Expose intent and behavior, not internal Hook machinery.
Custom Hooks should have predictable cleanup semantics.
A focused Hook is easier to test and reuse than a giant all-purpose Hook.

sections.title: Memoization Is Not a Semantic Cache
sections.content:
A memoized calculation should never be required for correctness. React may render in ways that make relying on memoization as persistent storage inappropriate.

If data must persist for correctness, use state, refs, or an appropriate external store. If recalculation is merely expensive, memoization may be useful after measurement.
keyTakeaways: Use memoization for performance, never as the source of truth.
Choose state or refs based on semantics.

sections.title: Hook Dependency Design
sections.content:
When a Hook has too many dependencies, do not automatically suppress the lint rule. First determine whether the Hook is doing too much, whether a callback can be moved inside the Effect, whether a functional state update can remove a dependency, or whether the external synchronization should be split.

Dependency complexity is often an architecture signal.
keyTakeaways: Dependency arrays expose the design of synchronization.
Large dependency lists can indicate that an Effect owns too many responsibilities.

sections.title: Imperative Handles
sections.content:
Imperative handles provide a controlled escape hatch for parent-to-child commands. A good handle exposes semantic operations such as `focus`, `scrollToError`, or `open`, not raw internal state.

Keep the imperative API minimal because it bypasses some of React's declarative data flow.

codeExample.title: Imperative Handles — Example
codeExample.explanation: A practical example of the concept.

keyTakeaways: Expose narrow commands rather than internal implementation.
Prefer declarative props when they can express the requirement.

chapters.title: Context, Global State, and Application Architecture
chapters.summary: Understand when state belongs locally, when to lift it, when Context is appropriate, and when a dedicated state library becomes valuable.

sections.title: Choosing the Owner of State
sections.content:
The most important state-management decision is ownership. Keep state as close as possible to the components that need it.

If two siblings need the same value, lift the state to their common parent. If unrelated areas need it across a large tree, consider Context or an external store.

Not every shared value is global state. Server data, URL state, form state, UI state, and durable client preferences have different lifecycles and often deserve different solutions.

codeExample.title: Choosing the Owner of State — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Prefer the narrowest state owner that satisfies the sharing requirement.
Different categories of state often need different storage strategies.
Avoid making every value global just because global state is available.

sections.title: Context: Dependency Injection for React Trees
sections.content:
Context lets a component read a value supplied by a provider higher in the tree without passing it through every intermediate component.

It is excellent for values such as theme, locale, authenticated user information, or service configuration that many descendants need.

Context is not automatically a replacement for every state library. When a context value changes, consumers that read it can rerender. Splitting contexts by responsibility and keeping provider values stable can reduce unnecessary work.

codeExample.title: Context: Dependency Injection for React Trees — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Context removes prop drilling for values shared through a tree.
Context consumers subscribe to the context value they read.
Separate unrelated contexts rather than creating one giant application context.

sections.title: External Stores and `useSyncExternalStore`
sections.content:
React can subscribe to data that lives outside React. `useSyncExternalStore` provides a standard subscription model that lets React safely read an external store.

This is useful for libraries or application infrastructure where state is intentionally maintained outside component state.

The store should expose a current snapshot and a subscription function. React can then coordinate reads and updates correctly with its rendering model.

codeExample.title: External Stores and `useSyncExternalStore` — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: External stores are useful when state ownership intentionally lives outside React.
`useSyncExternalStore` provides a React-aware subscription contract.
Do not build an external store simply to avoid learning React state.

sections.title: Server State Is Not the Same as Client State
sections.content:
Server data has characteristics that ordinary UI state does not: caching, freshness, deduplication, retries, pagination, invalidation, optimistic updates, and synchronization with a remote authority.

A common architecture mistake is copying every API response into a global Redux-like store and manually recreating a cache. Data-fetching libraries can provide those semantics directly.

Keep UI concerns such as selected tabs and dialog visibility separate from remote-resource concerns such as product lists and user profiles.

codeExample.title: Server State Is Not the Same as Client State — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Server state has caching and synchronization requirements beyond ordinary UI state.
Separate server-resource lifecycle from local UI state.
Choose a state solution based on the problem rather than popularity.

chapters.title: Data Fetching, Loading States, and Suspense
chapters.summary: Build resilient async UI with loading, error, empty, and success states, understand request lifecycles, and learn where Suspense fits.

sections.title: Model Async UI as States
sections.content:
A network request is not just “data or no data.” The UI may be idle, loading, successful, empty, failed, refreshing, or partially available.

Representing these states explicitly prevents contradictory combinations such as showing a success message while an old error remains visible.

For more complex resources, a reducer or server-state library can model transitions more clearly than a collection of unrelated boolean states such as `isLoading`, `hasError`, and `isEmpty`.

codeExample.title: Model Async UI as States — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Explicit async states prevent impossible UI combinations.
Loading, error, empty, success, and refreshing are distinct UX states.
As complexity grows, model transitions explicitly instead of adding more booleans.

sections.title: Fetching in Effects: Correctness First
sections.content:
Directly fetching from an Effect is possible, but the component must handle cancellation, stale responses, loading state, errors, and caching if needed.

For application-scale fetching, a dedicated server-state solution is often preferable because it solves many of these problems systematically.

If you do fetch in an Effect, make the request lifecycle explicit and avoid setting state after the request is no longer relevant.

codeExample.title: Fetching in Effects: Correctness First — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Check HTTP success explicitly; `fetch` does not reject for normal HTTP error statuses.
Abort obsolete requests when the resource identity changes.
Prefer established server-state abstractions when caching and synchronization become complex.

sections.title: Suspense as a Rendering Coordination Primitive
sections.content:
`Suspense` lets a part of the tree declare a fallback while something it depends on is not ready according to a Suspense-aware mechanism.

It is useful for coordinating loading UI around lazy-loaded components and, in frameworks that support it deeply, data and server rendering.

Suspense should not be confused with a universal replacement for loading state. Its usefulness depends on the data-fetching and rendering architecture around it.

codeExample.title: Suspense as a Rendering Coordination Primitive — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Suspense coordinates fallback UI around Suspense-enabled work.
`React.lazy` is a common client-side Suspense use case.
Suspense is an architectural primitive, not merely a prettier spinner.

sections.title: Error Boundaries
sections.content:
Render-time errors in a subtree can be isolated with an Error Boundary. This lets an application display fallback UI instead of losing the entire interface.

Error boundaries are different from `try/catch` around JSX. A `try/catch` in a component does not generally catch errors thrown later during rendering of child components.

A production application should decide where failures should be isolated: at route boundaries, feature boundaries, or other meaningful recovery units.

codeExample.title: Error Boundaries — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Error boundaries isolate rendering failures in descendant trees.
Use boundaries at meaningful recovery boundaries rather than only at the application root.
Log enough context to diagnose the failed feature without exposing sensitive data.

sections.title: Request Deduplication
sections.content:
Multiple components can request the same resource simultaneously. A production data layer can deduplicate requests so one network operation satisfies multiple consumers.

Without deduplication, dashboards can accidentally generate repeated calls for the same user, settings, or product data.
keyTakeaways: Query identity enables deduplication.
Server-state libraries often provide this behavior automatically.

sections.title: Stale-While-Revalidate
sections.content:
A cache can show known data immediately while refreshing it in the background. This creates a fast UI without pretending cached data is always current.

The UI should distinguish known stale data from a first-load empty state when that distinction matters to the user.
keyTakeaways: Stale data can be useful if its freshness is understood.
Refreshing and first loading are different UX states.

sections.title: Pagination and Infinite Scrolling
sections.content:
Pagination changes query identity because page or cursor becomes part of the resource. Infinite scrolling additionally needs to preserve previous pages while loading the next page.

Cursor-based APIs are often more stable than offset pagination when records can change while a user is browsing.
keyTakeaways: Pagination parameters belong in the resource identity.
Infinite lists require explicit loading and end-of-list states.

sections.title: Optimistic Mutation Rollback
sections.content:
Optimistic updates require a rollback strategy. Store enough previous information to restore the UI if the server rejects the operation.

After success, reconcile with the server response because the final authoritative representation may differ from the optimistic assumption.
keyTakeaways: Optimism requires rollback and reconciliation.
The server response remains authoritative.

chapters.title: React Performance and Rendering Optimization
chapters.summary: Learn how to diagnose slow renders, reduce unnecessary work, use memoization intelligently, virtualize large lists, and avoid accidental performance regressions.

sections.title: What Actually Makes a React App Slow?
sections.content:
React performance problems usually come from one of several categories: expensive calculations, too many components rendering, large DOM trees, excessive network work, large JavaScript bundles, or expensive browser layout/paint.

Do not start with `useMemo` and `useCallback`. First identify whether the bottleneck is rendering, computation, network, JavaScript execution, or browser work.

React DevTools Profiler can show which components rendered and how much time was spent. Browser Performance tools can reveal long tasks, layout, paint, and scripting costs.

codeExample.title: What Actually Makes a React App Slow? — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Measure the bottleneck before choosing an optimization.
React render time is only one part of browser performance.
Performance work should reduce a measured cost without making the code unnecessarily difficult to maintain.

sections.title: Memoized Components and Referential Equality
sections.content:
`React.memo` can skip a child render when its props are considered equal to the previous props.

This makes referential equality important. A newly created object, array, or function is a new reference even if it contains the same values.

Memoization can therefore fail when a parent creates new object props every render. But stabilizing every object and callback is not automatically beneficial; it can add complexity and memory overhead.

codeExample.title: Memoized Components and Referential Equality — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: `React.memo` is based on prop comparison.
Object and function identity can affect whether memoized children rerender.
Use memoization where it addresses a measured rendering cost.

sections.title: Large Lists and Virtualization
sections.content:
Rendering thousands of DOM nodes at once can be expensive even if React itself is efficient.

Virtualization renders only the items currently visible or near the viewport. This can dramatically reduce DOM size and layout work for large collections.

The key architectural idea is that the user cannot interact with thousands of visible rows simultaneously. Render the useful window, not the entire dataset.

codeExample.title: Large Lists and Virtualization — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Large DOM trees can become a browser performance problem.
Virtualization reduces the number of mounted rows.
For production, prefer a well-tested virtualization implementation over ad hoc scroll math.

sections.title: Code Splitting and Lazy Loading
sections.content:
A large JavaScript bundle delays startup because the browser must download, parse, and execute code before the application becomes interactive.

Dynamic imports let bundlers split code into chunks that can be loaded when needed. React's `lazy` works naturally with Suspense for component-level code splitting.

Route-level splitting is often a strong default because users do not need every feature's JavaScript on the first screen.

codeExample.title: Code Splitting and Lazy Loading — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Code splitting reduces initial JavaScript work.
Route and feature boundaries are natural split points.
A smaller initial bundle can improve startup even when total downloaded code remains similar.

sections.title: Transitions and Deferred Rendering
sections.content:
Some updates are urgent because they directly respond to typing or clicking. Other updates are expensive and can be allowed to yield to more urgent interactions.

React transitions let you mark certain updates as non-urgent. `useDeferredValue` can also let an expensive part of the UI lag behind an urgent input.

These tools do not make expensive computations intrinsically faster. They improve responsiveness by giving React more flexibility over when non-urgent work is rendered.

codeExample.title: Transitions and Deferred Rendering — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Transitions prioritize responsiveness; they do not reduce the algorithmic cost of work.
`useDeferredValue` allows a value consumer to lag behind an urgent value.
Use scheduling primitives when the problem is responsiveness rather than raw computation.

sections.title: Context and Render Granularity
sections.content:
Broad context values can cause many consumers to rerender when one field changes. Splitting contexts by responsibility or using selectors can improve granularity.

However, the goal is not zero renders. A small cheap rerender is often preferable to a complex architecture introduced solely to avoid it.
keyTakeaways: Optimize render cost, not render count alone.
Keep subscriptions aligned with actual dependencies.

sections.title: Browser Layout and Paint
sections.content:
React can finish quickly while the browser remains slow because of layout, paint, large shadows, expensive filters, or DOM size.

Use browser performance tools to identify long tasks and layout/paint bottlenecks before changing React code.
keyTakeaways: Browser rendering is part of frontend performance.
Measure the actual bottleneck.

sections.title: Worker-Based Computation
sections.content:
Very CPU-heavy client computations can block the main thread even when React scheduling is correct. A Web Worker can move computation off the main UI thread.

This introduces serialization and communication costs, so it is appropriate only when the computation is sufficiently expensive.

codeExample.title: Worker-Based Computation — Example
codeExample.explanation: A practical example of the concept.

keyTakeaways: Use workers for truly CPU-heavy browser work.
Measure transfer and serialization overhead.

chapters.title: Routing, Accessibility, and UI Architecture
chapters.summary: Design route-aware React applications and build interfaces that work with keyboards, screen readers, focus management, and semantic HTML.

sections.title: Client-Side Routing
sections.content:
A client-side router maps URLs to UI states. Routing is not merely a navigation component: it affects data loading, code splitting, error boundaries, authorization, document metadata, and browser history.

A route should represent a meaningful application state. Nested routes can mirror nested UI, while route parameters identify resources.

Always consider direct navigation and browser refresh. A production server must be configured to serve the application's entry point for client-managed routes when using an SPA architecture.

codeExample.title: Client-Side Routing — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: URLs should represent meaningful application states.
Dynamic route parameters identify resources.
SPA deployments need server fallback handling for direct route requests.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization Boundaries
sections.content:
Authentication answers “who is this user?” Authorization answers “what may this user do?”

A client-side protected route is useful for user experience, but it is not a security boundary. A malicious client can modify JavaScript or directly call APIs.

Real authorization must be enforced on the server or trusted backend. The frontend should still hide unavailable UI and redirect users to appropriate screens, but that is a presentation concern.

callout.title: Security rule
callout.message: Never treat a React conditional such as `if (user.isAdmin)` as proof that an operation is authorized. The backend must validate permissions.

codeExample.title: Authentication and Authorization Boundaries — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Frontend route guards improve UX but do not secure backend resources.
Authorization must be enforced at the API or trusted server boundary.
Separate authentication from authorization in both architecture and code.

sections.title: Semantic HTML Before ARIA
sections.content:
Accessibility starts with choosing the correct HTML element. A `<button>` already provides keyboard behavior and semantics that a clickable `<div>` does not.

Use headings in a meaningful hierarchy, labels for form controls, lists for lists, navigation landmarks for navigation, and buttons for actions.

ARIA is valuable when native HTML cannot express the required widget semantics, but adding ARIA to poorly structured HTML does not automatically make the interface accessible.

codeExample.title: Semantic HTML Before ARIA — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Use native semantic elements whenever possible.
Every form control should have an accessible name.
ARIA supplements HTML semantics; it does not replace correct HTML.

sections.title: Keyboard Navigation and Focus Management
sections.content:
Single-page applications can change content without a full browser navigation. That means focus can remain on a removed element or fail to move to the meaningful new content.

Dialogs, menus, route changes, and validation failures often need explicit focus management.

When building a dialog, manage focus into the dialog, keep keyboard interaction predictable, and return focus to the triggering element when the dialog closes.

codeExample.title: Keyboard Navigation and Focus Management — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Focus is part of application state and must be managed intentionally in dynamic UIs.
Keyboard users must be able to reach and operate interactive controls.
Dialogs should have a clear accessible name and predictable focus behavior.

chapters.title: Testing React Applications
chapters.summary: Learn what to test, how to test behavior rather than implementation details, and how unit, integration, component, and end-to-end tests fit together.

sections.title: Test Behavior, Not Component Internals
sections.content:
A robust React test asks what a user can observe or what a system boundary guarantees. It should avoid coupling itself to private state variables or implementation-specific component structure.

If a button says “Save”, a useful test clicks it and verifies the resulting behavior. A fragile test may inspect the component's internal state or require a specific DOM nesting that users do not care about.

This style makes refactoring safer because implementation can change while behavior remains constant.

codeExample.title: Test Behavior, Not Component Internals — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Prefer user-visible behavior over implementation details.
Accessible queries often produce resilient tests.
Tests should give confidence against regressions without blocking harmless refactors.

sections.title: Unit, Integration, and End-to-End Tests
sections.content:
Unit tests isolate small pieces of logic. Integration tests verify that multiple pieces work together. End-to-end tests exercise the application through a browser-like user journey.

React applications benefit from a balanced test pyramid. Pure domain logic can be tested cheaply. Important component interactions deserve integration coverage. Critical journeys such as login, checkout, or permissions deserve end-to-end coverage.

Do not maximize test count. Maximize confidence per test.

codeExample.title: Unit, Integration, and End-to-End Tests — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Use unit tests for isolated deterministic logic.
Use integration tests for important component and service interactions.
Use end-to-end tests for critical user journeys and deployment-level behavior.

sections.title: Testing Async UI
sections.content:
Async UI should be tested by waiting for observable results rather than forcing implementation-specific timing.

Avoid arbitrary sleeps such as `await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 1000))`. They make tests slow and flaky.

Instead, trigger the interaction and wait for the UI to reach the expected state. Mock network boundaries where appropriate, but preserve realistic request and response behavior in integration tests.

codeExample.title: Testing Async UI — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Wait for observable UI states instead of arbitrary timeouts.
Test loading, success, error, and empty states deliberately.
Keep network mocking at a clear boundary so tests remain understandable.

sections.title: Designing React Code for Testability
sections.content:
Testability is an architecture property. Components become easier to test when domain logic is separated from presentation and external services are accessed through explicit boundaries.

A component that directly contains validation, API calls, transformation logic, navigation, analytics, and rendering can become difficult to test and change.

Extract pure functions and domain services where they represent meaningful concepts. Keep components responsible primarily for translating state and user interactions into UI.

codeExample.title: Designing React Code for Testability — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Separate pure domain rules from UI rendering.
Explicit boundaries make dependencies easier to replace in tests.
Do not create abstractions merely for testing; extract concepts that are useful in production architecture.

sections.title: Testing Reducers and Pure Functions
sections.content:
Reducers are deterministic and should have direct unit tests for each meaningful action and edge case. This is often more valuable than rendering a full component for every state transition.

Pure validation, selectors, formatting, and transformation logic can similarly be tested without React.

codeExample.title: Testing Reducers and Pure Functions — Example
codeExample.explanation: A practical example of the concept.

keyTakeaways: Test deterministic logic directly.
Keep component tests focused on integration and user behavior.

sections.title: Testing Error Paths
sections.content:
Production failures often happen in paths that happy-path tests ignore. Test rejected requests, invalid input, permission failures, empty results, retries, and partial UI failures.

A mature suite treats failure states as first-class behavior.
keyTakeaways: Test failure and recovery paths explicitly.
Error states are part of the product contract.

sections.title: Flaky Test Diagnosis
sections.content:
Flaky tests often come from arbitrary timing, shared mutable state, leaked subscriptions, incomplete cleanup, network dependence, or selectors tied to unstable markup.

A flaky test should be fixed rather than repeatedly retried. Retries can hide genuine regressions.
keyTakeaways: Remove timing assumptions and shared state.
Retries should not be used to mask nondeterminism.

chapters.title: Advanced React Architecture
chapters.summary: Explore concurrent rendering concepts, server/client boundaries, framework architecture, hydration, design systems, feature organization, and production patterns.

sections.title: Concurrent Rendering as Scheduling
sections.content:
Concurrent rendering allows React to work on rendering without assuming every render must finish synchronously before other work can be considered.

The practical takeaway is not that React runs components on multiple CPU threads. Instead, React can schedule and interrupt rendering work so urgent interactions can remain responsive.

APIs such as transitions communicate priority. This is especially useful when an interaction starts expensive UI work that should not block typing or direct manipulation.

codeExample.title: Concurrent Rendering as Scheduling — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Concurrent rendering is primarily about scheduling and responsiveness.
A transition marks updates as non-urgent.
Concurrency does not mean component functions execute simultaneously on multiple threads.

sections.title: Server Rendering and Hydration
sections.content:
With server rendering, HTML can be generated before the browser executes the client JavaScript. Hydration then attaches React behavior to the server-rendered output.

Hydration requires the client render to agree with the server-rendered markup. Non-deterministic values such as random numbers, current timestamps, or environment-dependent branches can create mismatches.

Frameworks can manage much of this complexity, but the mental model remains important when debugging hydration warnings.

codeExample.title: Server Rendering and Hydration — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Hydration connects client React behavior to existing server-rendered markup.
Server and client output must be compatible.
Avoid non-deterministic rendering that changes markup between environments.

sections.title: Server and Client Component Boundaries
sections.content:
Modern React frameworks can split work between server-rendered components and interactive client components. A server component can keep server-only concerns away from the browser bundle, while a client component handles state, events, and browser APIs.

The boundary should be intentional. Data can often be fetched closer to where it is available, while interactivity is isolated to smaller client components.

Do not treat server/client boundaries as a replacement for application architecture. They are another dimension of the architecture that affects data flow, bundling, and execution environment.

codeExample.title: Server and Client Component Boundaries — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Server/client boundaries determine where code executes and what reaches the browser.
Keep interactive behavior in client components where the framework requires it.
Move data access toward the environment that can perform it securely and efficiently.

sections.title: Feature-Oriented Project Structure
sections.content:
As an application grows, organizing everything by technical type can create huge folders such as `components`, `hooks`, `services`, and `utils` with unrelated features mixed together.

Feature-oriented organization keeps UI, state, API adapters, tests, and domain logic near the feature that owns them.

The exact structure should reflect team boundaries and deployment needs. The goal is discoverability and ownership, not following a universal folder template.

codeExample.title: Feature-Oriented Project Structure — Example
codeExample.code:
src/
  app/
  features/
    billing/
      components/
      hooks/
      api/
      billing.test.js
    profile/
      components/
      api/
  shared/
    ui/
    lib/
  routes/
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Organize code around ownership and business boundaries as complexity grows.
Keep feature-specific code close to the feature.
Use shared folders for genuinely shared concepts, not as a dumping ground.

sections.title: Design Systems and Component APIs
sections.content:
A design system should provide stable primitives such as Button, Input, Dialog, Stack, and Text while allowing product features to compose them.

Good component APIs encode constraints that should be consistent across the product, such as focus behavior, disabled semantics, keyboard interactions, and visual variants.

Avoid turning the design system into a universal component with hundreds of props. When a component has too many unrelated responsibilities, split it into primitives and compositions.

codeExample.title: Design Systems and Component APIs — Example
codeExample.explanation: The example demonstrates the core idea described in this section.

keyTakeaways: Design-system components should provide reliable semantics and interaction behavior.
Keep component APIs constrained around coherent responsibilities.
Composition is usually more scalable than an enormous prop matrix.

sections.title: Server and Client Responsibility
sections.content:
Modern React architecture can divide work by execution environment. Server-side code can access private resources and perform data fetching, while client components handle interactivity.

This boundary should be explicit because moving code to the client can increase bundle size and expose dependencies that were previously server-only.
keyTakeaways: Execution environment is an architectural concern.
Keep privileged operations on trusted infrastructure.

sections.title: Designing for Change
sections.content:
A production architecture should make likely changes cheap. If billing rules change frequently, billing logic should have a clear boundary. If multiple teams own different features, code ownership should mirror those boundaries.

Architecture is therefore a prediction about future change, not only a description of today's folders.
keyTakeaways: Optimize boundaries around ownership and change.
Avoid abstractions that have no stable concept behind them.

sections.title: Avoiding Premature Abstraction
sections.content:
Duplicated code is not always a problem. Two similar components may diverge because they represent different concepts.

Extract an abstraction when the behavior is genuinely shared and likely to evolve together. Otherwise, premature abstraction can make independent features harder to change.
keyTakeaways: Abstract stable concepts, not superficial similarity.
Duplication can be cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

chapters.title: SSR, SSG, Streaming, Hydration, and Rendering Strategies
chapters.summary: Compare client rendering, server rendering, static generation, streaming, hydration, and hybrid rendering, including tradeoffs for SEO, performance, caching, and infrastructure.

sections.title: Client-Side Rendering
sections.content:
In client-side rendering, the browser receives JavaScript and constructs much of the UI on the client. This can provide rich interactivity but may delay meaningful content while JavaScript downloads and executes.

CSR is appropriate for authenticated dashboards and applications where SEO and first-content requirements are less important, but it should still be evaluated against startup cost.
keyTakeaways: CSR shifts rendering work to the browser.
Initial JavaScript cost can dominate startup performance.

sections.title: Server-Side Rendering
sections.content:
SSR generates HTML on the server for a request. The browser can display useful markup before hydration completes.

SSR introduces server execution cost, caching complexity, and hydration constraints. It is not automatically faster for every application.
keyTakeaways: SSR can improve initial content availability.
Server rendering introduces infrastructure and consistency requirements.

sections.title: Static Generation
sections.content:
Static generation produces HTML ahead of requests. It works especially well for content that changes less frequently and can be regenerated or revalidated.

Static output can be served from a CDN with very low latency, but highly dynamic data may require another rendering strategy.
keyTakeaways: Static generation is excellent for cacheable content.
Choose regeneration or dynamic rendering when freshness requirements demand it.

sections.title: Hydration Mismatches
sections.content:
Hydration requires compatible server and client output. Problems commonly come from browser-only APIs, random values, timestamps, locale differences, or conditional rendering based on environment.

A clean solution is to render deterministic server output and move browser-specific behavior to a client-side lifecycle after hydration when appropriate.

codeExample.title: Hydration Mismatches — Example
codeExample.explanation: A practical example of the concept.

keyTakeaways: Server output should be deterministic.
Browser-only values should be handled deliberately.

sections.title: Streaming and Progressive UI
sections.content:
Streaming allows independent portions of a response to arrive progressively. Suspense boundaries provide natural units for this progressive rendering.

A good streaming design avoids making the whole page wait for one slow dependency when independent content can be displayed earlier.
keyTakeaways: Design Suspense boundaries around independent user-perceived regions.
Streaming works best when slow dependencies are isolated.

sections.title: Rendering Strategy Selection
sections.content:
There is no universal best rendering mode. Public marketing pages may favor static or server rendering, authenticated dashboards may favor client rendering, and mixed applications can combine strategies.

Choose based on freshness, SEO, personalization, infrastructure, latency, and bundle constraints.

diagram.title: Rendering Strategy Decision
diagram.code:
flowchart TD
A[Page Requirements] --> B{Highly Dynamic?}
B -->|No| C[Static / Cached Rendering]
B -->|Yes| D{SEO / First Content Important?}
D -->|Yes| E[Server / Streaming Rendering]
D -->|No| F[Client Rendering]
C --> G[CDN Cache]
E --> H[Hydration / Client Boundaries]
F --> I[Browser Bundle]

keyTakeaways: Rendering strategy is a product and infrastructure decision.
Hybrid architectures are often the most practical.

chapters.title: Accessible Component Systems and Design Systems
chapters.summary: Go beyond individual accessibility fixes and design reusable React primitives with semantic behavior, keyboard interactions, focus management, theming, and API consistency.

sections.title: Button, Link, and Navigation Semantics
sections.content:
Buttons perform actions; links navigate. Using the wrong element creates keyboard, semantics, and assistive technology problems.

A design system should make the correct element easy to use rather than encouraging teams to style generic elements into fake controls.
keyTakeaways: Use buttons for actions and links for navigation.
Design-system primitives should preserve native semantics.

sections.title: Accessible Dialog Architecture
sections.content:
Dialogs require an accessible name, modal semantics when appropriate, keyboard escape behavior, focus entry, focus containment where required, and focus restoration.

A reusable Dialog component should own these behaviors so product teams do not implement them differently across the application.
keyTakeaways: Accessibility behavior belongs in reusable primitives.
Visual appearance and interaction semantics are separate concerns.

sections.title: Tabs, Menus, and Comboboxes
sections.content:
Composite widgets have keyboard interaction models that are significantly more complex than ordinary buttons. Tabs need selection and arrow-key behavior; menus have roving focus patterns; comboboxes combine text input with a popup list and active option semantics.

Prefer established accessible patterns and test them with keyboards and assistive technology.
keyTakeaways: Composite widgets require deliberate keyboard contracts.
Do not invent accessibility interaction rules casually.

sections.title: Design Tokens and Theming
sections.content:
A design system can expose semantic tokens such as `surface`, `text`, `danger`, and `focusRing` rather than raw colors. This supports themes and accessibility adjustments.

React Context can provide theme configuration, while CSS variables can efficiently implement the actual visual tokens.

codeExample.title: Design Tokens and Theming — Example
codeExample.explanation: A practical example of the concept.

keyTakeaways: Prefer semantic design tokens.
Use CSS variables for efficient theme application.

sections.title: Component Contracts
sections.content:
Reusable components should define what they guarantee: keyboard behavior, focus behavior, ARIA semantics, disabled behavior, controlled state, and visual variants.

A component is successful when consumers can rely on its contract without reading its implementation.
keyTakeaways: Document behavior, not only props.
Stable contracts make design systems scalable.

chapters.title: Security, Observability, and Production Reliability
chapters.summary: Protect React applications against XSS and client-side trust mistakes while building error reporting, logging, monitoring, deployment, and resilience practices.

sections.title: XSS and Raw HTML
sections.content:
React escapes text interpolation, but `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` intentionally bypasses this safety. If rich HTML is required, sanitize it using a trusted sanitizer and define a strict content policy.

Never assume data is safe because it came from your own database. Stored malicious content can become an XSS vector later.
keyTakeaways: Treat rich HTML as untrusted until sanitized.
Stored XSS can persist long after the original input.

sections.title: CSRF and Authentication Architecture
sections.content:
Authentication mechanisms have different CSRF characteristics. Cookie-based sessions require careful CSRF defenses because browsers attach cookies automatically. Token-based designs have their own storage and XSS tradeoffs.

The frontend should not decide security policy by itself; it should cooperate with a trusted backend security model.
keyTakeaways: Authentication and browser credential transport must be designed together.
Do not store sensitive credentials casually in browser-accessible storage.

sections.title: Error Monitoring
sections.content:
Production error monitoring should capture stack traces, release versions, route information, and safe contextual metadata. Source maps can make minified production stack traces actionable.

Avoid collecting passwords, tokens, private message contents, or unnecessary personal data.
keyTakeaways: Observability should be actionable and privacy-aware.
Release identifiers are critical for connecting errors to deployments.

sections.title: Feature Flags
sections.content:
Feature flags allow gradual rollout, experimentation, and rapid disablement. Flags introduce branching complexity, so they need ownership, expiration, and cleanup.

A flag that lives indefinitely becomes a permanent second architecture.
keyTakeaways: Feature flags are temporary architecture unless intentionally permanent.
Remove stale flags and dead branches.

sections.title: Production Error Boundaries
sections.content:
Place boundaries around features where recovery is possible. A dashboard widget can fail without taking down the whole dashboard.

A boundary should offer useful recovery such as retrying the feature, navigating away, or reporting the failure.
keyTakeaways: Failure isolation should match product boundaries.
A global boundary should be a last line of defense, not the only boundary.

chapters.title: Advanced Component Patterns and API Design
chapters.summary: Master compound components, headless components, controlled/uncontrolled APIs, portals, imperative handles, render props, and reusable stateful abstractions.

sections.title: Compound Components
sections.content:
Compound components form a family of components that share state and coordinate behavior. Context is commonly used internally to avoid manually passing state between every member.

This pattern creates expressive APIs such as `<Tabs><Tabs.List>...</Tabs.List></Tabs>` while keeping related behavior encapsulated.
keyTakeaways: Compound components work well for cohesive widget families.
Keep implicit relationships documented.

sections.title: Headless Components
sections.content:
A headless component provides behavior and accessibility while leaving visual rendering to the consumer. This is useful for design systems serving multiple brands or applications.

Headless components need strong contracts because consumers control more of the DOM.
keyTakeaways: Separate interaction behavior from visual styling when reuse demands it.
Accessibility remains the responsibility of the behavior layer.

sections.title: Portals
sections.content:
Portals change where children are mounted in the DOM while preserving React ownership. They are useful for overlays that should escape clipping and stacking contexts.

A portal does not automatically provide modal accessibility or focus management.

codeExample.title: Portals — Example
codeExample.explanation: A practical example of the concept.

keyTakeaways: Portals are useful for overlays.
Focus and keyboard behavior still need explicit handling.

sections.title: Controlled and Uncontrolled APIs
sections.content:
A reusable component can support both controlled and uncontrolled operation. The controlled mode receives its value and change callback from the parent; the uncontrolled mode owns internal state and accepts a default value.

The API should define what happens if consumers switch between modes, because silently changing ownership can create confusing behavior.
keyTakeaways: Controlled mode delegates ownership to the parent.
Uncontrolled mode lets the component own state.

sections.title: Imperative APIs
sections.content: Imperative handles are useful for commands such as focusing an input or scrolling a validation error into view. They should expose semantic operations rather than raw DOM nodes whenever possible.
keyTakeaways: Expose narrow imperative capabilities.
Prefer declarative APIs for ordinary state changes.

sections.title: Reusable State Machines
sections.content:
Complex widgets can separate interaction state from rendering. A reducer or state machine can describe valid transitions, while React renders the current state.

This makes the interaction logic reusable across multiple visual presentations.
keyTakeaways: Separate complex interaction rules from presentation when reuse warrants it.
Explicit transitions make edge cases easier to test.

chapters.title: Top Interview Questions & Practice
chapters.summary: Master 60 essential React interview questions ranging from core fundamentals to senior-level real-world scenarios.

sections.title: Junior Fundamentals
sections.content: Core JSX, components, props, state, and rendering. Explain why the correct option is correct and why the alternatives are weaker.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the primary programming model React encourages?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: React encourages declarative UI: describe what the UI should look like for the current state and let React reconcile that description with the host environment.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is JSX?
options: JavaScript syntax for describing UI elements
interactiveQuiz.explanation: JSX is syntax that is transformed into JavaScript representations of React elements. It is not HTML executed directly by the browser.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why are keys needed when rendering lists?
options: To identify list items across renders
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Keys provide identity for sibling elements in a collection so React can reason about which items were inserted, removed, or moved.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the recommended source of truth for a controlled input?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A controlled input gets its value from React state and reports changes through an event handler.

interactiveQuiz.question: What happens when a state setter is called?
options: The current render variable is mutated immediately
React requests an update and a future render can observe the new state
interactiveQuiz.explanation: State is associated with renders. Calling a setter schedules an update; the current render's state variable remains its existing snapshot.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which is the correct way to update state based on previous state?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The functional updater receives the latest queued state value, making it correct when multiple updates depend on previous state.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does a component normally return?
options: A description of UI such as React elements
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A React component returns a description of the UI it wants React to render.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why should state objects generally not be mutated directly?
options: Immutable updates make state transitions and identity changes predictable
Objects cannot be passed as props
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Creating new references for changed state makes updates predictable and avoids mutating snapshots that other code may still reference.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is a prop?
options: A value passed from a component to its descendant
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Props are inputs supplied by a parent component to a child component.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is `children` in React?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `children` is a normal React prop populated by content placed between a component's opening and closing tags.

interactiveQuiz.question: When should you generally use `useEffect`?
options: To synchronize with an external system
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Effects are intended for synchronization with external systems such as subscriptions, timers, browser APIs, and imperative widgets.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is a stale closure in a React Effect?
options: A callback reading values from an older render
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Functions created during a render close over that render's values. If synchronization is incorrect, an asynchronous callback can keep reading an outdated value.

interactiveQuiz.question: What should cleanup from an Effect normally do?
options: Reverse or cancel the resource created by the Effect
Set every state variable to null
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Cleanup should undo the external synchronization: unsubscribe, clear a timer, abort a request, remove a listener, and so on.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does `useRef` return?
options: A stable ref object whose current value can change without causing a render
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A ref object persists across renders. Changing `.current` does not itself trigger a React render.

interactiveQuiz.question: When is `useReducer` especially useful?
options: For related state with explicit transitions
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Reducers are useful when state transitions are related and can be expressed as explicit actions.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the main purpose of a custom Hook?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Custom Hooks encapsulate reusable stateful behavior and can combine React's built-in Hooks.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why must Hooks not be called conditionally?
options: Because JSX cannot contain if statements
React relies on consistent Hook call order
Hooks only work in class components
interactiveQuiz.explanation: React associates Hook state with call order. Conditional calls can change that order between renders.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does `useMemo` return?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useMemo` caches the result of a calculation until its dependencies change.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does `useCallback` primarily memoize?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useCallback` returns a cached function reference based on its dependencies.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which statement about memoization is best?
options: Every component should use all memoization Hooks
Memoization should address measurable work or identity-sensitive boundaries
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Memoization has a cost. It is most useful when it prevents meaningful work or stabilizes identity across an important boundary.
